sounds.name: THE SOUND [a]

spellings.condition: in some words when followed by a double m or n

notes.text: *In phonetics, the â is a slightly different sound than [a]. It is the sound [ɑ], which is considered ‘anterior’ (the tongue is placed further back in the mouth). But nowadays, this particular pronunciation is rare, and in those words, the â is often pronounced [a]. **oi isn't just the [a] sound but a combination of [w] and [a]: [wa] ([w] is a semi-vowel that you’ll learn about later in this chapter).

notes.text: The pronunciation of ai is generally [ɛ], but in some instances it is pronounced as [e]. le plaisir [lə pleziʀ] → pleasure This sound can also vary in the same verb depending on the conjugation: • it can be [ɛ]: j’aide [jɛd] → I help • or [e]: vous aidez [vuzede] → you (plural) help Additionally, the pronunciation of ai in some words varies among native speakers, depending on their regional accent or the context. For example, you may hear the word “maison” (house) pronounced [mezɔ̃] or [mɛzɔ̃].

sounds.name: OPEN O [ɔ]

spellings.condition: in the middle of a syllable

analogy.text: With a more open mouth; similar to pronouncing the o in “from”.

sounds.how_to: With a more open mouth; similar to pronouncing the o in “from”.

notes.text: • Some words borrowed from other languages can have the sound [ɔ] written as oo. l’alcool [lalcɔl] → alcohol • The distinction between the open o [ɔ] and the closed o [o] varies according to regions and accents. Listen to the difference in pronunciation of this sentence between someone from Paris and someone from the South of France: “J’aime les fleurs roses et jaunes.” • Parisian accent: [ʒɛm le flœʀ ʀozeʒon] • Southern accent: [ʒemə le flœʀə ʀɔzə e ʒɔnə] French people who live in the south of France tend to pronounce the closed o [o] as an open o [ɔ], the sound ai [e] instead of [ɛ]. They also often pronounce the silent e in many words, adding more syllables to sentences, so the rhythm of their French is closer to Italian.

spellings.condition: in front of a p, b or m

sounds.how_to: Your lips are spread as for the sound [ɛ] (è), your mouth is slightly open, and your tongue is up front, touching your bottom teeth. The air should be coming out through both the mouth and the nose. (Try to pinch your nose; if the sound changes, that means you are doing it right!)

notes.text: The sounds [ɛ̃] and [œ̃] are very similar and are often confused. The difference in pronunciation will be mainly regional. For example, in northern France, these two sounds tend to be pronounced the same, whereas in southern France, you’ll hear a difference in their pronunciation.

notes.text: In certain words, we pronounce the letter C as [s], even when followed by a, o, u. To indicate that the letter c is to be pronounced [s] and not [k], a cedilla, a mark derived from the Latin alphabet, is added under the letter c: c → ç la France [la fʀɑ̃s] → une française [yn fʀɑ̃sɛz] – France, a French person (feminine) j’avance [ʒavɑ̃s] → nous avançons [nuzavɑ̃sɔ̃] – I move forward, we move forward → the spelling “qu” also makes a [k] sound. sounds.name: The Pronunciation of R in French
sounds.how_to: It may surprise you, but the French R is closer to the consonant sound [g] than to the English R. Pronounce the [g] sound twice, then keep the same position of your mouth and tongue and pronounce the [ʀ] sound now by producing a vibration in your throat.
sounds.intro: The consonant R is the most frequent consonant in French. The R can be pronounced in four different ways, depending on the country and region where French is spoken, and also depending on where the R is positioned within a word. No matter how R is pronounced, the meaning of the word does not change. All the different ways to pronounce it can be represented by these phonetic symbols: [ʁ] [χ] [r] [ʀ] Listen to this sentence une prune ronde (a round plum) pronounced with the different R: [ʁ] [χ] [r] [ʀ] However, like many French dictionaries, in our phonetic transcriptions, we have written every R [ʀ], regardless of the difference in pronunciation, in order to simplify reading the phonetic transcription and because these different R are considered 'allophone', which means that no matter which way (out of the four) you decide to pronounce the R, it won't change the meaning of the word. Romain, regarde ces trois gros radis rouges, rajoute du sel et dévore-les, c’est merveilleux tu vas voir ! [ʀɔmɛ̃ / ʀəgaʀd se tʀwa gʀo ʀadi ʀuʒ / ʀaʒut dy sɛl e devɔʀ le / sə mɛʀvejø ty va vwaʀ] Romain, look at these three big red radishes, add some salt and devour them, you’ll see it’s wonderful!

general.heading: Les Voyelles Orales, Nasales et les Semi-Voyelles
general.text: Oral, Nasal Vowels and Semi-Vowels Vowels are classified as oral, nasal, or semi-vowels according to the tongue's placement in the mouth (its height, position at the front or back of the mouth) and whether or not the lips are rounded. In French, various spellings can represent the same vowel sound. That's why it's essential to learn the different ways a vowel sound can appear in a French word.

general.heading: THE SOUNDS ‘EUH’ [ø], [œ], [ə]
general.text: French has three types of “EUH” sounds: one is closed [ø], one is more open [œ], and the third [ə] is silent or nearly silent.

general.heading: Les Voyelles Nasales
general.text: Nasal Vowels Among the ten French vowel sounds absent in English, four are nasal vowels. Nasal sounds occur when air exits through the nasal passages and the mouth during speech. The IPA symbol for a nasal vowel is a tilde [~] over the corresponding oral vowel.

general.heading: HOW TO PRONOUNCE NASAL VOWELS?
general.text: The sound must pass through the mouth and nose at the same time. If you touch your nostrils when you pronounce a nasal vowel, you should feel the vibration and air coming out.

general.heading: Les Semi-Voyelles Semi-Vowels
general.text: French has three semi-vowels (sometimes called semi-consonnes in French): these sounds are created by the partial obstruction of air through the throat and mouth.

general.heading: Les Consonnes Consonants
general.text: To pronounce consonants, you need to block or hinder the passage of air through the mouth. For example, to pronounce [p], you need to close your lips briefly before forcing air through, whereas for a vowel sound like [a], your mouth remains open. As we mentioned in the introduction, out of the 18 consonant sounds in French, 16 are the same as in English, but with some slight differences in the pronunciation: → The consonant sounds in French are more rapid and require greater tension in the muscles of the mouth than in English. → Some letters are pronounced more in the front of the mouth in French. The sounds of the letters D, L, N, and T are very similar in French and English, except that in French, the tip of your tongue touches the back of your front teeth (dental sound), whereas in English, it is slightly farther back (on the roof of your mouth, just behind your teeth). la danse [la dɑ̃s] dance [ˈdɑːns] une tarte [yn taʀt] a tart [eɪˈtɑːrt] (When you pronounce the French words, your tongue should be farther forward than for the English words.) → The letters P , B and K are pronounced similarly in French and English, except that in French, they are not aspirated (less air is expelled) when it’s at the beginning of a word. In English, you can hear a puff of air following these letters, but not in French. la peinture [la pɛ̃tyʀ] paint [ˈpeɪnt] un bateau [œ̃ bato] a boat [eɪˈbəʊt] (If you were to place a piece of paper in front of your mouth and pronounce those words, the paper should only move with the English words.)
